rewritten_text:
I rushed to her, gathered her into my arms, and covered her with caresses, pleading:

“Speak, darling, tell me! What is it?”

Her head dropped limply against my chest, and she gasped so softly I could barely hear:

“HELLO-CENTRAL!”

“Quick!” I shouted to Clarence. “Call the king’s homeopath and tell him to come!”

Within two minutes I was kneeling beside the child’s crib while Sandy sent servants racing in every direction through the palace. One glance almost told me everything: membranous croup! I leaned over and whispered:

“Wake up, sweetheart! Hello-Central.”

She slowly opened her gentle eyes and managed to say:

“Papa.”

That reassured me. She was a long way from dead. I ordered sulfur preparations brought and dug out the croup kettle myself. When Sandy or the child is ill, I don’t sit waiting for doctors. I knew how to nurse them both, and I had experience. This little creature had spent much of her short life in my arms. Often I could ease her distress and make her laugh, with tears still glistening on her eyelashes, even when her mother couldn’t.

Just then Sir Launcelot strode down the great hall in his finest armor, heading for the stock exchange. He was its president and held the Siege Perilous, which he had purchased from Sir Galahad. The exchange consisted of the Knights of the Round Table, and these days they used the Round Table for business. A seat there cost—well, you wouldn’t believe the amount, so there’s no point naming it. Sir Launcelot was a bear. He had cornered the market in one of the new lines and was preparing to squeeze the short sellers that very day. But what did that matter? He was still the old Launcelot. As he passed the doorway, he looked in and discovered that his little favorite was ill. That settled it. The bulls and bears could settle their battles however they liked; he would come in and stand by little Hello-Central with everything he had. And he did. He tossed his helmet into a corner, and within half a minute had fitted a fresh wick to the alcohol lamp and was heating the croup kettle. Meanwhile Sandy had arranged blankets into a canopy above the crib, and everything was ready.

Sir Launcelot raised the steam. Together we charged the kettle with unslaked lime and carbolic acid, adding a little lactic acid, then filled it with water and slipped the steam spout beneath the canopy. Everything was properly arranged now, and we seated ourselves on opposite sides of the crib to keep watch.

On the hearth lay two or three long, thick locks of gray human hair, stained with blood and apparently torn out by the roots. On the floor were four Napoleon coins, a topaz earring, three large silver spoons, three smaller spoons of Algerian metal, and two bags holding almost four thousand francs in gold. A chest of drawers stood in one corner. Its drawers were open and seemed to have been searched, though many things remained inside. Beneath the bedding—not beneath the bed frame—was a small iron safe. It stood open, its key still in the lock. Inside were only a few old letters and other unimportant papers.

“No sign of Madame L’Espanaye was found here. But an unusually large amount of soot in the fireplace led to a search of the chimney. From it, horrible as it is to tell, they pulled the daughter’s body, head down. Someone had forced her a considerable distance up the narrow opening. Her body was still quite warm. Examination showed many scrapes, undoubtedly caused by the force used to push her in and pull her out. There were deep scratches on her face. Her throat had dark bruises and deep fingernail marks, suggesting that she had been strangled.

“After searching every part of the house thoroughly and finding nothing more, the group went into a small paved yard behind the building. The old woman’s body lay there. Her throat had been cut so completely that when they tried to lift her, her head fell off. Both her head and body were terribly mutilated. The body was so badly damaged that it scarcely looked human.

“We believe there is still not the slightest clue to this dreadful mystery.”

The following day’s newspaper supplied these further details.

“‘The Tragedy in the Rue Morgue.’ Many people have been questioned about this extraordinary and horrifying affair”—the French word ‘affaire’ does not yet carry the frivolous meaning it has for us—“but nothing has emerged to explain it. Below we print all the relevant witness statements.

“Pauline Dubourg, a laundress, states that she knew both women for three years and did their washing throughout that time. The old woman and her daughter appeared to get along well and were very loving toward each other. They always paid her well. She could say nothing about how they lived or supported themselves. She believed Madame L. earned her living by telling fortunes. People said the old woman had money saved.”

He sprang up and grabbed her arm roughly. “Show him to me. Which one is he? Point him out. I have to see him!” he cried. But just then the Duke of Berwick’s carriage, drawn by four horses, blocked their view. By the time it passed, the other carriage had driven out of the park.

“He’s gone,” Sibyl said sadly. “I wish you could have seen him.”

“So do I. As surely as there’s a God in heaven, if he ever hurts you, I’ll kill him.”

She stared at him in horror. He said it again, his words slicing the air like a knife. People nearby began to stare. A woman beside her gave a little laugh.

“Come away, Jim. Come away,” she whispered. He followed stubbornly as she made her way through the crowd. He was glad he had said it.

At the statue of Achilles, she turned to him. The pity in her eyes turned to laughter on her lips. She shook her head. “You’re foolish, Jim, completely foolish. You’re just a bad-tempered boy. How can you say such terrible things? You don’t know what you’re talking about. You’re being jealous and unkind. Oh, I wish you would fall in love! Love makes people good, and what you said was wicked.”

“I’m sixteen,” he replied, “and I know what I’m doing. Mother’s no help to you. She doesn’t know how to take care of you. Now I wish I weren’t going to Australia at all. I’m very tempted to give the whole thing up. I would, if I hadn’t signed my contract.”

“Oh, don’t be so serious, Jim. You sound like a hero in one of those silly melodramas Mother loved acting in. I’m not going to argue with you. I’ve seen him, and seeing him is perfect happiness! We won’t argue. I know you’d never hurt anyone I love, would you?”

“Not while you still love him, I suppose,” he answered sulkily.

“I’ll love him forever!” she cried.

“And him?”

“Forever too!”

“He’d better.”

She drew back from him. Then she laughed and rested her hand on his arm. He was only a boy.

At Marble Arch they caught a bus that dropped them near their shabby home on Euston Road. It was past five, and Sibyl needed to lie down for a couple of hours before her performance. Jim insisted that she rest. He said he would rather say goodbye to her without their mother there. Their mother was bound to make a scene, and he hated scenes of any kind.
